title: Proof of the Circle Theorems Flashcards

cards.front: All radii of the same circle are [ ___ ], so a triangle made from two radii is [ ___ ].
cards.back: All radii of the same circle are equal, so a triangle made from two radii is isosceles.

options.text: All radii of the same circle are equal, so a triangle made from two radii is isosceles.
options.explanation: Radii from the centre to the circumference have the same length. Therefore, a triangle containing two radii has two equal sides and is isosceles.

options.text: All radii of the same circle are equal, so a triangle made from two radii is equilateral.
options.explanation: Two radii provide only two known equal sides; the chord joining their endpoints need not have the same length. The triangle is therefore isosceles, not necessarily equilateral.

options.text: All radii of the same circle are unequal, so a triangle made from two radii is scalene.
options.explanation: This reverses the defining property of a circle: every radius of one circle has equal length. The two equal radii therefore form an isosceles triangle.

options.text: All radii of the same circle are perpendicular, so a triangle made from two radii is right-angled.
options.explanation: Radii are equal in length, but they are not generally perpendicular to one another. Their equality makes the triangle isosceles; the central angle can have many values.

cards.front: In triangle $AOB$ where $OA=OB$, what angle equality follows?
cards.back: $\angle OAB=\angle ABO$.

options.explanation: Since $OA=OB$, triangle $AOB$ is isosceles with base $AB$. The angles opposite those equal sides, $\angle OAB$ and $\angle ABO$, are equal.
This incorrectly equates the vertex angle with a base angle. Since $OA=OB$, the equal opposite angles are $\angle OAB$ and $\angle ABO$.
Equal sides produce equal angles opposite them, not an equality involving the included angle at $O$. Therefore $\angle OAB=\angle ABO$.
This would require $OB=AB$, which is not given. The stated equality $OA=OB$ makes their opposite angles equal, so $\angle OAB=\angle ABO$.

cards.front: The angle at the centre is [ ___ ] the angle at the circumference when both stand on the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both stand on the same arc.

options.text: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both stand on the same arc.
options.explanation: The centre-angle theorem states that angles subtended by the same arc satisfy this $2:1$ relationship: the central angle is twice the corresponding circumference angle.

options.text: The angle at the centre is equal to the angle at the circumference when both stand on the same arc.
options.explanation: This confuses the theorem with equal angles in the same segment. For the same arc, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.

options.text: The angle at the centre is three times the angle at the circumference when both stand on the same arc.
options.explanation: The multiplier is incorrectly taken as three. Splitting the proof into isosceles triangles shows that the central angle is exactly twice the circumference angle.

options.text: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both stand on the different arcs.
options.explanation: The $2:1$ relationship applies only when both angles are subtended by the same arc. Angles standing on different arcs do not generally have this relationship.

cards.front: In the centre-angle proof, if $\angle PQO=x$, why is $\angle OPQ=x$?
cards.back: $OP=OQ$, so triangle $OPQ$ is isosceles.

options.explanation: Both $OP$ and $OQ$ are radii of the same circle, so they are equal. Their opposite base angles, $\angle PQO$ and $\angle OPQ$, are therefore equal.
This selects the wrong pair of equal sides and would equate different opposite angles. The radii are $OP$ and $OQ$, so $OP=OQ$ gives the required base-angle equality.
The chord $PQ$ is not generally equal to the radius $OQ$. The known equal sides are the radii $OP$ and $OQ$, making the angles at $P$ and $Q$ equal.
The radii need not meet at a right angle, and right-angled triangles do not automatically have equal acute angles. The equality follows from $OP=OQ$ and the isosceles triangle theorem.

cards.front: In triangle $OPQ$, if the base angles are both $x$, what is $\angle POQ$?

options.explanation: The angles in a triangle total $180^\circ$. Subtracting the two base angles, $x+x=2x$, leaves $\angle POQ=180^\circ-2x$.
This subtracts only one of the two base angles. Since both base angles equal $x$, their total is $2x$, giving $\angle POQ=180^\circ-2x$.
This incorrectly uses the $360^\circ$ total around a point instead of the $180^\circ$ angle sum of a triangle. The correct angle is $180^\circ-2x$.
This incorrectly assumes the triangle’s angles total $90^\circ$. A triangle’s interior angles total $180^\circ$, so subtracting both base angles gives $180^\circ-2x$.

cards.front: In the centre-angle proof, what central angle is obtained after subtracting $180^\circ-2x$ and $180^\circ-2y$ from $360^\circ$?

options.explanation: The required central angle is $360^\circ-(180^\circ-2x)-(180^\circ-2y)$. The constant terms cancel, leaving $2x+2y$.
This loses the factors of two when simplifying the two isosceles-triangle angles. Subtracting both expressions from $360^\circ$ gives $2x+2y$, twice the circumference angle.
This subtracts the variable terms instead of subtracting each entire bracket. Expanding the subtraction changes their signs, so the result simplifies to $2x+2y$.
This uses $180^\circ$ rather than the full $360^\circ$ around the centre and mishandles the bracket signs. Correct subtraction gives the central angle $2x+2y$.

cards.front: If $\angle PQO=x$ and $\angle OQR=y$, what is $\angle PQR$?

options.explanation: The ray $QO$ divides $\angle PQR$ into the adjacent angles $\angle PQO=x$ and $\angle OQR=y$. Adding them gives $\angle PQR=x+y$.
Adjacent parts of the same larger angle must be added, not subtracted. Since $QO$ splits $\angle PQR$ into angles $x$ and $y$, the total is $x+y$.
This mistakenly applies the centre-angle doubling rule to the circumference angle itself. The two adjacent components at $Q$ simply add, so $\angle PQR=x+y$.
This treats the three angles as though they formed a triangle angle sum. Here $x$ and $y$ are adjacent parts of $\angle PQR$, so the angle is $x+y$.

cards.front: If a line passes through [ ___ ] and both ends lie on the circle, it is a [ ___ ].
cards.back: If a line passes through the centre and both ends lie on the circle, it is a diameter.

options.text: If a line passes through the centre and both ends lie on the circle, it is a diameter.
options.explanation: A chord whose endpoints lie on the circumference and which passes through the circle’s centre is a diameter. It is also the longest possible chord.

options.text: If a line passes through the centre and both ends lie on the circle, it is a radius.
options.explanation: A radius has only one endpoint on the circumference and ends at the centre. With both endpoints on the circle and the centre between them, the line is a diameter.

options.text: If a line passes through a point inside and both ends lie on the circle, it is a diameter.
options.explanation: Passing through any interior point is insufficient; many ordinary chords do this. The line is specifically a diameter only when it passes through the centre.

options.text: If a line passes through the centre and both ends lie on the circle, it is a tangent.
options.explanation: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and does not have two endpoints on the circumference. A chord through the centre is a diameter.

cards.front: In the semicircle proof, why does $\angle AOB+\angle BOC=180^\circ$?
cards.back: $AOC$ is a straight line.

options.explanation: Points $A$, $O$ and $C$ are collinear because $AC$ is a diameter. Therefore the adjacent central angles $ngle AOB$ and $ngle BOC$ form a straight angle of $180^\circ$.
The chord $AB$ does not generally pass through the centre, so it is not necessarily a straight line through $O$. The angles total $180^\circ$ because $AOC$ is a straight line.
The radii $OA$ and $OB$ make triangle $AOB$ isosceles, but this does not make the two central angles supplementary. Their sum is $180^\circ$ because $AOC$ is a straight line.
Equal radii make $OA=OC$, but equality of lengths does not establish a sum of angles. The adjacent angles total $180^\circ$ because $AOC$ is a straight line.

cards.front: What does $(180^\circ-2x)+(180^\circ-2y)=180^\circ$ give for $x+y$?
cards.back: $x+y=90^\circ$.

options.explanation: Expanding and simplifying gives $360^\circ-2x-2y=180^\circ$, so $2x+2y=180^\circ$. Dividing every term by $2$ gives $x+y=90^\circ$.
This misses the final division by $2$. Simplification gives $2x+2y=180^\circ$, and dividing both sides by $2$ gives the correct result $x+y=90^\circ$.
This treats the original $180^\circ$ total as though it were $360^\circ$. Correctly collecting terms gives $2x+2y=180^\circ$, hence $x+y=90^\circ$.
This incorrectly halves the result twice. Once $2x+2y=180^\circ$ has been obtained, a single division by $2$ gives $x+y=90^\circ$.

cards.front: In a semicircle, the angle on the circumference opposite the diameter is [ ___ ].
cards.back: In a semicircle, the angle on the circumference opposite the diameter is $90^\circ$.

options.explanation: The angle in a semicircle theorem states that an angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the remaining circumference is a right angle, so it equals $90^\circ$.
A diameter subtends $180^\circ$ at the centre, not at the circumference. The corresponding angle on the circumference is half the central angle, so it is $90^\circ$.
This results from halving the circumference angle rather than the central angle. The diameter subtends $180^\circ$ at the centre, so the circumference angle is $90^\circ$.
This confuses the semicircle theorem with an equilateral-triangle angle. A diameter subtends a right angle at the circumference, so the required angle is $90^\circ$.

cards.front: What can you conclude about two angles standing on the same chord on the same side of it?
cards.back: They are equal.

options.explanation: Angles subtended by the same chord in the same segment are equal. Both angles intercept the same endpoints and lie on the same side of the chord.
Supplementary angles arise as opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, not as angles in the same segment. Angles standing on the same chord on the same side are equal.
Complementary angles sum to $90^\circ$, which is associated with an angle in a semicircle. Angles standing on the same chord in the same segment are instead equal.
Perpendicular describes lines meeting at $90^\circ$, not a relationship between two angle sizes. Angles standing on the same chord on the same side are equal.

cards.front: Why are $\angle ABD$ and $\angle ACD$ equal when both stand on chord $AD$?
cards.back: Both are half of the same central angle, $\angle AOD$.

options.text: Both are half of the same central angle, $\angle AOD$.
options.explanation: Each circumference angle standing on chord $AD$ is half the central angle subtended by that chord. Since both are half of $ngle AOD$, they are equal.

options.text: Both are twice the same central angle, $ngle AOD$.
options.explanation: The central angle theorem has the relationship reversed here: the central angle is twice each circumference angle. Therefore both circumference angles are half of the same central angle, $ngle AOD$.

options.text: Both are equal to the same central angle, $ngle AOD$.
options.explanation: A circumference angle is not equal to the central angle subtended by the same chord. Each is half of the same central angle, $ngle AOD$, which proves they are equal.

options.text: Both are half of the same central angle, $ngle BOC$.
options.explanation: Chord $AD$ subtends the central angle $ngle AOD$, not $ngle BOC$. Both circumference angles are equal because each is half of $ngle AOD$.

cards.front: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on the [ ___ ] of a circle.
cards.back: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on the circumference of a circle.

options.explanation: A quadrilateral is cyclic precisely when each of its four vertices lies on one circle’s circumference. Its sides are chords joining pairs of those points.
The centre is a single point and cannot contain four distinct vertices of a quadrilateral. In a cyclic quadrilateral, all four vertices lie on the circle’s circumference.
The diameter is one particular chord through the centre, so four vertices cannot all lie on it and form a quadrilateral. They must lie on the circumference.
The radius is a line segment from the centre to the circumference, not the boundary containing all four vertices. A cyclic quadrilateral’s vertices lie on the circumference.

cards.front: In cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, what is $\angle ABC+\angle ADC$?

options.explanation: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary because the arcs subtending them together form the complete circle. Therefore, their angle sum is $180^\circ$.
This confuses supplementary opposite angles with complementary angles. In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles subtend arcs totalling $360^\circ$, so their angles sum to $180^\circ$.
This uses the angle sum around a point rather than the cyclic quadrilateral theorem. Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so the required sum is $180^\circ$.
This incorrectly subtracts a right angle from a full turn. The opposite angles of any cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, meaning their sum is exactly $180^\circ$.

cards.front: Why do opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$?
cards.back: Their central angles add to $360^\circ$, and circumference angles are half.

options.text: Their central angles add to $360^\circ$, and circumference angles are half.
options.explanation: The central angles corresponding to the two opposite circumference angles make one full turn, totalling $360^\circ$. Each circumference angle is half its central angle, so their sum is $180^\circ$.

options.text: Their central angles add to $180^\circ$, and circumference angles are half.
options.explanation: The two relevant central angles complete a full turn, not a straight angle, so they total $360^\circ$. Halving that total gives the opposite circumference angles’ sum of $180^\circ$.

options.text: Their central angles add to $360^\circ$, and circumference angles are double.
options.explanation: The central angle is twice the angle at the circumference, so the relationship has been reversed. The central angles total $360^\circ$, and their half-sized circumference angles total $180^\circ$.

options.text: Their central angles add to $180^\circ$, and circumference angles are double.
options.explanation: Both relationships are reversed: the relevant central angles make a full $360^\circ$ turn, and circumference angles are half the corresponding central angles, producing a sum of $180^\circ$.

cards.front: What angle does a radius make with a tangent at the point of contact?

options.explanation: A radius is perpendicular to a tangent where the tangent touches the circle. Therefore, the angle between them at the point of contact is $90^\circ$.
Confusing the radius-tangent angle with an angle from an isosceles triangle can suggest $45^\circ$. A radius and tangent are perpendicular, so the correct angle is $90^\circ$.
An angle of $180^\circ$ forms a straight line, but a tangent does not continue along the radius. The radius meets the tangent perpendicularly at $90^\circ$.
An angle of $0^\circ$ would make the radius and tangent parallel or coincident. They are perpendicular at the point of contact, giving an angle of $90^\circ$.

cards.front: The tangent-chord theorem is also called the [ ___ ].
cards.back: The tangent-chord theorem is also called the alternate segment theorem.

options.explanation: The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and chord equals the angle subtended by that chord in the opposite segment.
The angle in the same segment theorem compares two angles subtended by the same chord. The tangent-chord result is instead called the alternate segment theorem.
The cyclic quadrilateral theorem concerns opposite angles adding to $180^\circ$, not an angle between a tangent and chord. The required name is the alternate segment theorem.
The angle at the centre theorem compares central and circumferential angles subtended by one arc. The tangent-chord theorem is also called the alternate segment theorem.

cards.front: What does the tangent-chord theorem say?
cards.back: The tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the opposite segment.

options.text: The tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the opposite segment.
options.explanation: For a chord through the point of contact, the angle between that chord and the tangent equals the angle subtended by the chord in the opposite segment.

options.text: The tangent-chord angle equals the angle at the centre.
options.explanation: The angle at the centre is generally twice the corresponding angle at the circumference, so it does not equal the tangent-chord angle. The opposite-segment angle does.

options.text: The tangent-chord angle equals twice the angle in the opposite segment.
options.explanation: The factor of two belongs to the angle at the centre theorem, not the tangent-chord theorem. The tangent-chord angle equals, rather than doubles, the opposite-segment angle.

options.text: The tangent-chord angle equals half the angle in the opposite segment.
options.explanation: Halving is used when deriving a circumference angle from the corresponding central angle. The tangent-chord angle directly equals the angle in the opposite segment.

cards.front: Why is the tangent-chord angle $90^\circ-y$ when $\angle OCB=y$?
cards.back: $$OC$ is perpendicular to the tangent, leaving $90^\circ-y$.

options.text: $$OC$ is perpendicular to the tangent, leaving $90^\circ-y$.
options.explanation: A radius meets a tangent perpendicularly, making a total angle of $90^\circ$. Since $\angle OCB=y$ occupies part of it, the remaining tangent-chord angle is $90^\circ-y$.

options.text: $$OC$ is perpendicular to the tangent, leaving $180^\circ-y$.
options.explanation: Perpendicular lines form $90^\circ$, not $180^\circ$. Subtracting $y$ from the right angle means the tangent-chord angle is $90^\circ-y$, rather than $180^\circ-y$.

options.text: $$OC$ is parallel to the tangent, leaving $90^\circ-y$.
options.explanation: A radius to the point of contact is perpendicular, not parallel, to the tangent. The right angle is split into $y$ and the remaining angle $90^\circ-y$.

options.text: $$OC$ is perpendicular to the tangent, leaving $90^\circ+y$.
options.explanation: The two adjacent angles must total $90^\circ$, so $y$ must be subtracted rather than added. Consequently, the tangent-chord angle is $90^\circ-y$.

cards.front: In the tangent proof, why is $\angle BAC=90^\circ-y$?
cards.back: It is half of $\angle BOC$, where $\angle BOC=180^\circ-2y$.

options.text: It is half of $\angle BOC$, where $\angle BOC=180^\circ-2y$.
options.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same chord. Halving $180^\circ-2y$ gives $\angle BAC=90^\circ-y$.

options.text: It is half of $\angle BOC$, where $\angle BOC=180^\circ-y$.
options.explanation: This omits the factor of $2$ multiplying $y$ in the central angle. Since $\angle BOC=180^\circ-2y$, halving it correctly gives $\angle BAC=90^\circ-y$.

options.text: It is equal to $\angle BOC$, where $\angle BOC=180^\circ-2y$.
options.explanation: An angle at the circumference is half, not equal to, the angle at the centre subtended by the same chord. Therefore, half of $180^\circ-2y$ gives $90^\circ-y$.

options.text: It is half of $\angle BOC$, where $\angle BOC=360^\circ-2y$.
options.explanation: Using $360^\circ$ incorrectly treats the relevant central angle as reflex. The interior central angle is $180^\circ-2y$, whose half is $90^\circ-y$.
